heading: The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout).
title: OSHA lockout tagout requirements (29 CFR 1910.147)
description: OSHA lockout tagout requirements in 29 CFR 1910.147: program, procedures, devices, training, inspections, citation data and a LOTO checklist.
opening: 29 CFR 1910.147 requires employers to run an energy control program (procedures, training and at least annual inspections) so machines are isolated from energy sources and made inoperative before servicing or maintenance where unexpected energization, start-up or release of stored energy could injure employees.

topIndustries.title: Machine Shops; Turned Product; and Screw, Nut, and Bolt Manufacturing

enforcementSummary: The most-cited paragraph is 1910.147(c)(4)(i), with 4,835 citations. It requires energy control procedures to be developed, documented and used. Next come (c)(6)(i), the periodic inspection of each procedure at least annually (3,061), and (c)(1), the overall energy control program (2,405), while the training paragraphs (c)(7)(i) and (c)(7)(i)(A) drew 1,963 and 1,574. Yearly citations rose from 3,777 in FY2022 to 4,746 in FY2025, and FY2026 recorded 4,429.
requirementsIntro: 1910.147 applies to servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment where unexpected start-up or stored energy could injure employees, with the exclusions listed in 1910.147(a)(1)(ii). The section runs from scope and definitions in (a) and (b), through program duties in (c), the application sequence in (d) and release in (e), to the additional situations in (f).

requirements.heading: Which work does OSHA 1910.147 cover?
requirements.intro: 1910.147 covers servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment that could energize, start up or release stored energy unexpectedly and injure employees, and it reaches normal production work only in the situations listed in (a)(2)(ii).

items.text: Servicing and maintenance are in scope wherever a machine could start up or energize unexpectedly, or release stored energy, and injure an employee.

Excluded: construction and agriculture employment; employment covered by parts 1915, 1917 and 1918; installations under the exclusive control of electric utilities for power generation, transmission and distribution; electrical hazards in electric-utilization installations covered by subpart S; and oil and gas well drilling and servicing.

Servicing during normal production is covered only if an employee must remove or bypass a guard or other safety device, or place any part of the body in the point of operation or an associated danger zone during a machine operating cycle.

Minor tool changes, adjustments and other minor servicing during normal production fall outside the standard only if they are routine, repetitive and integral to using the equipment for production, and are done with alternative measures that give effective protection (see subpart O).
Work on cord-and-plug equipment is not covered when unplugging controls the hazard and the plug stays under the exclusive control of the employee doing the servicing or maintenance.

Hot tap operations on pressurized pipelines carrying gas, steam, water or petroleum products are not covered only if the employer demonstrates that continuity of service is essential, shutdown is impractical, and documented procedures and special equipment with proven effective protection are used.

requirements.heading: What must an energy control program and its procedures contain?
requirements.intro: Under 1910.147(c)(1), the energy control program consists of energy control procedures, employee training and periodic inspections, so that each machine is isolated from its energy source and rendered inoperative before servicing or maintenance where unexpected energizing, start-up or release of stored energy could cause injury.

items.text: Procedures for controlling potentially hazardous energy must be developed, documented and used whenever employees do work covered by the standard.

A procedure need not be documented for a particular machine only when all eight conditions in the exception exist, among them no potential for stored or residual energy, a single readily identified energy source, a single lockout device under the authorized employee's exclusive control, and no past accidents from unexpected activation or reenergization during servicing or maintenance.
Procedures must clearly and specifically set out scope, purpose, authorization, rules, techniques and the means to enforce compliance, including a specific statement of intended use.
Each procedure gives specific steps for shutting down, isolating, blocking and securing the machine.
Steps for placing, removing and transferring lockout or tagout devices, and who is responsible for them, must be written into the procedure.
The procedure must state requirements for testing the machine to verify that locks, tags and other energy control measures work.
Where another standard in Part 1910 requires lockout or tagout, the procedural and training requirements of 1910.147 apply on top of it.

requirements.heading: When may tagout be used instead of lockout?
requirements.intro: Lockout is required on an energy isolating device that is capable of being locked out unless the employer demonstrates that tagout gives full employee protection, and a tagout system is used where the device cannot take a lock.

items.text: If an energy isolating device is not capable of being locked out, the program must use a tagout system.
If the device is capable of being locked out, the program must use lockout unless the employer can demonstrate that tagout provides full employee protection as set out in (c)(3).
A tag used on a lockable device goes at the same location the lock would have been attached, and the employer must show the tagout program gives safety equivalent to lockout.

That showing requires full compliance with all tagout-related provisions plus additional measures, such as removing an isolating circuit element, blocking a controlling switch, opening an extra disconnecting device or removing a valve handle.
After January 2, 1990, energy isolating devices must be designed to accept a lockout device whenever a machine is replaced, undergoes major repair, renovation or modification, or is newly installed.
Push buttons, selector switches and other control circuit type devices do not count as energy isolating devices.

requirements.heading: What must lockout and tagout devices look like?
requirements.intro: Under 1910.147(c)(5), the employer supplies the locks, tags and hardware, and every lockout or tagout device must be durable, standardized, substantial and identifiable.

items.text: The employer provides locks, tags, chains, wedges, key blocks, adapter pins, self-locking fasteners or other hardware for isolating, securing or blocking machines.
Devices must be singularly identified, be the only devices used for controlling energy, and not be used for other purposes.

Devices must withstand their environment for the longest expected exposure, and tags must not deteriorate or become illegible in weather, wet or damp locations, or corrosive areas where acids and alkalis are handled.
Devices are standardized within the facility by color, shape or size, and tags are also standardized in print and format.
Lockout devices must resist removal except by excessive force or unusual techniques such as bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools.

Tag attachments must be non-reusable, attachable by hand, self-locking and non-releasable, with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds, at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie.
Each lockout or tagout device must show who applied it.
Tags must warn against hazardous conditions if the machine is energized and carry a legend such as Do Not Start, Do Not Open, Do Not Close, Do Not Energize or Do Not Operate.

requirements.heading: How often must energy control procedures be inspected?
requirements.intro: 1910.147(c)(6)(i) requires a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually, carried out by an authorized employee other than those using the procedure being inspected.

items.text: The inspection is done at least annually to confirm that the procedure and the standard are being followed.
The inspector must be an authorized employee who is not one of the people using the procedure under inspection.
The inspection is conducted to correct any deviations or inadequacies it identifies.
Where lockout is used, the inspector reviews each authorized employee's responsibilities under the procedure with that employee.
Where tagout is used, the review covers each authorized and affected employee and also the tag limitations listed in (c)(7)(ii).
The employer certifies each inspection, naming the machine, the date, the employees included and the person who performed it.

requirements.heading: What training and retraining does 1910.147 require?
requirements.intro: Training under 1910.147(c)(7) differs by role, with separate content for authorized employees, affected employees and other employees who work where energy control may be used, and the employer must certify it.

items.text: Authorized employees are trained to recognize applicable hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of energy in the workplace, and the methods for energy isolation and control.
Affected employees are instructed in the purpose and use of the energy control procedure.
All other employees whose work is or may be in an area where energy control may be used are instructed about the procedure and the ban on trying to restart locked-out or tagged-out machines.
Where tagout systems are used, employees are also trained in the limitations of tags, including that tags give no physical restraint and may create a false sense of security.
Authorized and affected employees are retrained when their job assignment changes, when machines, equipment or processes change in a way that presents a new hazard, or when the procedures change.
Additional retraining is required when a periodic inspection reveals, or the employer has reason to believe, that an employee's knowledge or use of the procedures has deviations or inadequacies.
The employer certifies that training is done and kept up to date, recording each employee's name and dates of training.

requirements.heading: In what order must lockout or tagout be applied and removed?
requirements.intro: 1910.147(d) sets a fixed sequence for applying energy control, and 1910.147(e) sets the checks an authorized employee completes before devices come off and energy is restored.

items.text: Only the authorized employees performing the servicing or maintenance may apply lockout or tagout.
The employer or authorized employee notifies affected employees before controls are applied and after they are removed.

The sequence is: preparation (knowing the type and magnitude of the energy, its hazards and how to control it), orderly shutdown, isolation, device application, relief of stored energy, then verification.
Authorized employees affix a lockout or tagout device to each energy isolating device.
If stored energy could reaccumulate to a hazardous level, verification of isolation continues until the work is complete or that possibility no longer exists.
Before work starts, the authorized employee verifies that isolation and deenergization have been accomplished.
Before release, the work area is inspected so nonessential items are removed and components are operationally intact, and all employees are confirmed safely positioned or removed.

Each device is removed by the employee who applied it; if that person is unavailable, removal under the employer's direction needs a documented procedure and training giving equivalent safety, including verifying the person is not at the facility, making all reasonable efforts to contact them, and making sure they know before resuming work there.

requirements.heading: What extra rules cover testing, contractors, group lockout and shift changes?
requirements.intro: 1910.147(f) adds requirements for temporarily re-energizing to test or position a machine, for outside contractors, for crews working under group lockout or tagout, and for shift or personnel changes.

items.text: To test or position a machine, clear tools and materials, remove employees, remove devices as (e)(3) specifies, energize and test, then deenergize and reapply controls under (d) before servicing continues.
When outside servicing personnel do covered work, the on-site and outside employers must inform each other of their lockout or tagout procedures.
The on-site employer ensures its own employees understand and comply with the restrictions and prohibitions of the outside employer's program.
A crew, craft or department doing servicing uses a procedure that protects each worker as well as a personal lockout or tagout device would.
Primary responsibility for a set number of employees under a group device, such as an operations lock, rests with one authorized employee.
Where more than one crew, craft or department is involved, an authorized employee is designated to coordinate the work forces and ensure continuity of protection.
Each authorized employee puts a personal lock or tag on the group lockout device or lockbox when starting work and removes it when stopping work on that machine.
Specific procedures, including orderly transfer of device protection between off-going and oncoming employees, keep protection continuous through shift or personnel changes.

checklistIntro: This checklist covers the 1910.147 program, devices, application, release, inspection and training records; use it for the annual periodic inspection or when spot-checking a lockout in progress.

faq.question: Is Appendix A to 1910.147 mandatory?
faq.answer: No. The note before Appendix A calls it a non-mandatory guideline that neither adds to nor detracts from the requirements. It gives a typical minimal lockout procedure employers can adapt, and it says more complex systems may need more comprehensive procedures.

faq.question: What is the difference between an authorized and an affected employee?
faq.answer: Under the definitions in 1910.147(b), an authorized employee locks or tags out a machine in order to service or maintain it. An affected employee operates or uses a machine being serviced under lockout or tagout, or works in the area where that servicing happens. An affected employee becomes an authorized employee once their duties include covered servicing or maintenance.

faq.question: Do blank flanges and slip blinds count as lockout devices?
faq.answer: Yes. The 1910.147(b) definition of a lockout device, a device using a positive means such as a key or combination lock to hold an energy isolating device in a safe position, expressly includes blank flanges and bolted slip blinds.

faq.question: Does cleaning or unjamming a machine count as servicing?
faq.answer: It does when the employee could be exposed to the machine energizing or starting unexpectedly, or to a release of hazardous energy. The 1910.147(b) definition of servicing and/or maintenance lists lubrication, cleaning, unjamming, adjustments and tool changes, along with constructing, installing, setting up, inspecting and modifying machines.
